## Today's question

On day 16 the treated seedlings grew on average **6.22 mm more** than the
controls. A second experiment with 24 new seedlings would give a different
number, so how much should we trust 6.22 mm? Today you add a **Welch two-sample
t-test** to `comparison.Rmd`. It gives the two numbers that every results
section reports next to an estimate: a **95% confidence interval** and a
**p-value**.

Open `comparison.Rmd` and run its chunks, so that `seedlings`, `treated` and
`control` exist. The study design is described in
[data/README.md](../data/README.md).

**Save today:** `comparison.Rmd` and its HTML, `day17-checks.R`, and an updated
`transfer-comparison.Rmd` with its HTML.

## Does the Welch test fit this study?

Each value in `treated` is the growth of one plant, and each value in `control`
is the growth of another plant. The plants were randomly allocated to the two
groups, so the groups are **independent**, which is what Welch's test needs. The
treated plants vary more (SD 4.87 mm) than the controls (SD 3.19 mm); that is
fine, because Welch's test does not assume equal spread. Look at the day 16
plot once more for a single plant far away from all others. There is none here,
so the test can go ahead.

## Running the test

```{r}
comparison <- t.test(treated, control, var.equal = FALSE,
                     alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)
comparison
```

`t.test()` subtracts the second vector from the first, so the result describes
**treated minus control**, the direction we chose on day 16. `var.equal = FALSE`
selects Welch's method (it is also R's default; writing it shows the reader
which test you used), `alternative = "two.sided"` counts a difference in either
direction, and `conf.level = 0.95` asks for a 95% interval. The
[R documentation for t.test](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/t.test.html)
lists all arguments.

You should see, among other lines:

```text
t = 3.7012, df = 18.986, p-value = 0.001517
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.700984 9.732349
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y
 21.49167  15.27500
```

## Reading the output

| R prints | Value | Units | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mean of x`, `mean of y` | 21.49, 15.28 | mm | Mean growth of treated and control plants |
| (subtract them) | **6.22** | mm | The estimate: treated − control |
| `95 percent confidence interval` | **2.70 to 9.73** | mm | Uncertainty in the mean difference |
| `t`, `df` | 3.70, 19.0 | none | Used to calculate the p-value |
| `p-value` | **0.0015** | none | How surprising the data would be if the means were equal |

Read the result in this order. The **estimate** says that treated plants grew
6.22 mm more on average in our sample. The **confidence interval** says that
population mean differences from about 2.70 to 9.73 mm fit the data; because
the whole interval lies above zero, the data point to more growth with the
treatment. The interval is about the *mean* difference, not about single
plants: several control plants grew more than several treated plants. If the
whole experiment were repeated many times, about 95% of such intervals would
contain the true difference.

The **p-value** answers a narrower question: if treated and control plants had
the same mean growth, how often would a difference at least this large appear
by chance? About 0.15% of the time, so rarely. This is not the probability that
the treatment has no effect, and it says nothing about whether 6 mm matters for
a seedling of about 20 mm. That judgement needs the estimate and biology.

## Writing the result in the report

Use `$` to take numbers out of the result instead of retyping them, so the
report stays correct if the data change:

```{r}
mean(treated) - mean(control)
comparison$conf.int
comparison$p.value
```

In `comparison.Rmd`, add a Methods sentence (two independent groups, growth =
final − initial, treated minus control, Welch two-sample t-test) and a Results
paragraph such as:

> Treated seedlings grew on average 6.22 mm more than controls (21.49 mm versus
> 15.28 mm, 12 plants per group; 95% confidence interval 2.70 to 9.73 mm;
> Welch two-sample t-test, p = 0.0015).

End with one sentence on the biological size of the difference and one on the
limits of this small simulated study. Keep the individual-point plot. Restart R
and render.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: what if an interval includes zero?

Zero means "no difference in mean growth". An interval from, say, −1 to 5 mm
contains both small negative and moderate positive differences, so the study
cannot tell the direction. Report it as inconclusive, not as "no effect".
:::

## Does the order of the groups matter?

In a new script, `day17-checks.R`, use `t.test(control, treated)` to find out
whether swapping the two groups changes the conclusion.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The interval becomes −9.73 to −2.70 mm: the same numbers with the opposite sign,
because it now describes control minus treated. The p-value stays 0.0015. The
data have not changed, only the direction in which we describe them, so keep
the treated-minus-control version in the report.
:::

## How sure is "95% sure"?

In `day17-checks.R`, use `t.test(treated, control, conf.level = 0.90)` and
`conf.level = 0.99` to find out how the range of plausible differences changes
when you ask for more or less confidence.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

90%: 3.31 to 9.12 mm. 95%: 2.70 to 9.73 mm. 99%: 1.41 to 11.02 mm. The more
confident you want to be that the interval contains the true difference, the
wider it must be. The means do not change. Keep 95% in the report: choose the
level before you look, not after.
:::

## Correcting wrong sentences

Each of these sentences, all common in student reports, contains one error.
Write a corrected version of each in `day17-checks.R` as a comment.

1. "There is a 0.15% probability that the treatment has no effect."
2. "95% of treated plants grew between 2.70 and 9.73 mm more."
3. "Another study found a 2 mm difference with a 95% interval of −1 to 5 mm, so
   the treatment does nothing."

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

1. The p-value is calculated *assuming* equal means: if the means were equal, a
   difference this large would appear in about 0.15% of experiments.
2. The interval is for the **mean** difference, not for individual plants.
3. The interval includes zero but also differences of up to 5 mm, so the study
   could not determine the direction. It is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect.
:::

## A second class's data

Another class repeated the experiment with nine plants per group
(`data/seedlings-transfer.csv`; you summarised it on day 16 in
`transfer-comparison.Rmd`). Use `t.test(new_treated, new_control)` to find out
whether treated plants also grew more in this study, and how precisely the
difference is estimated. Create the two vectors from `transfer` the same way
you created `treated` and `control`, then add the test and a results sentence
to `transfer-comparison.Rmd` and render it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer check

Mean growth was 17.87 mm (treated) and 13.66 mm (control): a difference of
**4.21 mm**, 95% CI **1.95 to 6.47 mm**, Welch p = **0.0012**. This interval is
narrower than the first study's (7.0 mm wide against 4.5 mm), even though each
group has three plants fewer, because these plants vary much less (SD 1.94 and
2.53 mm against 4.87 and 3.19 mm). Precision depends on both sample size and
spread.
:::

## Check your understanding

1. Which numbers have units of mm: the difference, the interval, or the p-value?
   **The difference and the interval; a p-value has no unit.**
2. Does the SD of a group describe the uncertainty in the difference? **No; SD
   describes how much single plants vary.**
3. If all treated plants had grown in one shared pot and all controls in
   another, would this test still fit? **No; the plants would no longer be
   independent units.**

**Leave with:** `comparison.Rmd` and its HTML reporting the estimate, interval,
p-value and sample sizes; `day17-checks.R`; and `transfer-comparison.Rmd` with
its HTML.
